\newcommand{\skillaxis}{competitive-programming difficulty}
\title{Does AI Code Detection Reduce to \emph{Skill} Detection?\\
\large A preliminary, two-sided answer}
\author{Autonomous experiment (Claude Code) for Matthew}
\date{\today}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We ask whether AI-code detectors track author \textbf{species} (human vs.\ LLM) or
author \textbf{skill/style}. Across \resNCf{} Codeforces Python samples (human solutions
stratified by problem difficulty; LLM solutions from \resNModels{} models under
natural/novice/expert prompts) and three detectors spanning the trained (DroidDetect)
and statistical (Fast-DetectGPT, Binoculars) families, the answer is two-sided.
\textbf{(1)} On the \skillaxis{} axis the confound is \emph{absent}: the skill-matched
vs.\ mismatched AUROC gap is $\Delta_{\text{confound}}\!\approx\!\resMeanDelta{}$, and
within-species score slopes run \emph{against} the naive skill prediction (mean human
slope $\resMeanHumanSlope{}$ SD). This vindicates the concern that terse
competitive-programming style is the stylistic \emph{opposite} of the idiomatic
``senior-engineer'' register that RLHF code models imitate.
\textbf{(2)} Yet on \resNLegendary{} samples of pre-LLM-era code from renowned engineers
(Torvalds' original \texttt{git}, antirez's Redis, Hipp's SQLite, CPython)---ironclad
human and contamination-free---the trained detector labels \textbf{\resLegFlagDroidNative{}}
of it AI at its native threshold. The confound is therefore \emph{real, but on the
idiomatic-polish axis}, which competitive rating fails to capture.
\end{abstract}

\section{Question and hypotheses}
Post-RLHF code models are tuned toward idiomatic, well-structured ``senior-engineer''
style. If detectors learned that style as the AI signal, then \emph{AI-vs-human}
detection partly reduces to \emph{expert-vs-novice} detection. We pre-registered:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{H$_\text{species}$}: detectors classify species; within-species skill has
        no effect (slopes $\approx 0$; AUROC constant across skill cells).
  \item \textbf{H$_\text{skill}$}: detectors classify skill; among humans, higher skill
        $\to$ more ``AI''; among LLMs, novice prompting $\to$ less ``AI''.
  \item \textbf{H$_\text{mixed}$}: a weighted combination.
\end{itemize}

\section{Data and methods}
\textbf{Human.} Accepted Python-3 Codeforces solutions (MatrixStudio), difficulty bands
easy ($\le 1200$) and hard ($\ge 1900$). \emph{Deviation from the original plan:} no public
dataset co-locates human source code with \emph{author} Elo, so the human skill axis is
problem difficulty---a noisy, and as it turns out stylistically \emph{inverted}, proxy.
\textbf{LLM.} \resNModels{} models (gemma-2-2b-it, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and the frontier
\texttt{gpt-5.4-nano}) under natural/novice/expert prompts on the same problems.
\textbf{Detectors} (oriented higher${}={}$more AI): DroidDetect-Base-Binary (trained);
Fast-DetectGPT and Binoculars (statistical; canonical vendored implementations).
\textbf{Stats.} AUROC is primary (threshold-free); all CIs use a cluster bootstrap over
\emph{problems}; the within-species score slope (z-scored detector output regressed on the
skill axis) is the mechanism test; $\Delta_{\text{confound}}$ is reported per detector.

\section{Results}

\subsection{The confound is absent on the competitive-skill axis}
Table~\ref{tab:slopes} gives within-species slopes (SD units). Under H$_\text{skill}$ both
columns should be positive; instead the human slope is \emph{negative} for DroidDetect
($\resHumanSlopeDroidDetect{}$, CI $[\resHumanSlopeLoDroidDetect{},\resHumanSlopeHiDroidDetect{}]$)
and Fast-DetectGPT ($\resHumanSlopeFastDetectGPT{}$), and null for Binoculars
($\resHumanSlopeBinoculars{}$). Higher \skillaxis{} skill is scored, if anything,
\emph{less} AI-like.

\midrule

Fast-DetectGPT & statistical & \resHumanSlopeFastDetectGPT{}  & \resLlmSlopeFastDetectGPT{}\\

The skill-matched vs.\ mismatched AUROC gap is essentially zero
(Table~\ref{tab:delta}): $\Delta_{\text{confound}}=\resDeltaDroidDetect{}$
(CI $[\resDeltaCIloDroidDetect{},\resDeltaCIhiDroidDetect{}]$) for DroidDetect, and
\resDeltaFastDetectGPT{} and \resDeltaBinoculars{} for the statistical detectors---i.e.\
matching humans and LLMs on competitive
skill does \emph{not} collapse detector performance. On this axis the data favour
H$_\text{species}$.

\subsection{But the confound is real on the idiomatic-polish axis}
On contamination-free pre-LLM elite code, DroidDetect labels \resLegFlagDroidNative{} of
samples AI at its native threshold, and \resLegFlagDroidDetect{} even at a threshold
calibrated to a 5\% false-positive rate on ordinary Codeforces humans---roughly an order
of magnitude above nominal. The effect is strongest on the most idiomatic code: CPython
library code is flagged at \resLegAuthorCPythonCore{} (5\% FPR), versus
\resLegAuthorLinusTorvalds{} for Torvalds' original \texttt{git} and
\resLegAuthorSalvatoreSanfilippo{} for Redis.

\begin{figure}[h]\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{fig4_legendary_flag_rates.png}
\caption{Pre-LLM elite human code flagged as AI (thresholds${}={}$5\% FPR on ordinary humans).}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Mechanism and confirmatory checks}
Surface style features explain $R^2=\resStyleRsqDroidDetect{}$ of DroidDetect's score and
$\resStyleRsqFastDetectGPT{}$ of Fast-DetectGPT's---style matters but does not fully
account for the trained detector. On the harder Codeforces problems human code is in fact
\emph{more} idiomatic (type-hint rate \resStyleHasTypeHintsEasy{}${}\to{}$%
\resStyleHasTypeHintsHard{}), which makes the negative human slope notable: more idiomatic
\emph{competitive} code is still not read as more AI.

A confirmatory cohort using real \emph{author} Elo (AtCoder; low band $n=\resAtNLowSkill{}$
mean Elo \resAtRatingLowSkill{}, high band $n=\resAtNHighSkill{}$ mean Elo
\resAtRatingHighSkill{}) points the same way: the high$-$low score gap is negative for all
detectors (e.g.\ DroidDetect \resAtHiLoDroidDetect{} SD), though the thin high band leaves
wide CIs.

\begin{figure}[h]\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.7\linewidth]{fig3_within_species_slopes.png}
\caption{Within-species slopes: detector score vs.\ skill, per species.}
\end{figure}

\section{Limitations}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Problem difficulty / competitive rating $\ne$ idiomatic-code skill.} This is
        now the central finding, not just a caveat: the proxy is stylistically inverted.
  \item \textbf{Accepted-only human code} is a collider (rating$\to$accept$\leftarrow$difficulty);
        LLM code is unfiltered---asymmetric.
  \item \textbf{Small LLM panel} (gemma-2-2b, Qwen2.5-3B, gpt-5.4-nano); preliminary $n$.
  \item \textbf{DroidDetect contamination} (Codeforces-like training data) not audited; the
        pre-LLM legendary probe is the contamination-free anchor.
  \item \textbf{Thin AtCoder high-skill band} ($n=\resAtNHighSkill{}$).
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}
``Does AI-code detection reduce to skill detection?'' \emph{Not} to competitive-programming
skill---there the confound is absent and the relationship mildly inverts, because terse
competitive style is the opposite of idiomatic style. But detection \emph{is} materially
confounded by \textbf{idiomatic code style}: a trained SOTA-style detector flags
\resLegFlagDroidNative{} of provably-human, pre-LLM, elite code as machine-generated. The
deployment risk is real---the most polished human engineers are the most likely to be
falsely accused---but the right axis to study it is production-code idiom, not competitive
rating. The clean follow-up is an author-reputation cohort on idiomatic production code
(e.g.\ GitHub by maintainer reputation) and a larger high-skill sample.
